subtopic: LEGISLATION REVISION COMMISSION
speechtext:
1.	Particular attention is being paid to the French text of the statutes in order to improve the expression of that text wherever corrections can be made within the limits of the powers of the Commission under Section 5 of 1964-65, c. 48.
2.	It was intended that the Revised Statutes would be available in the Fall of 1968. This may not now be achieved because of the continuation of the 1967 Session of Parliament into the year 1968.
3.	Until recently almost all Bills drafted in the Legislation Section were drafted in the first instance in English and then translated into French by translators carrying out the functions prescribed by the Translation Bureau Act (R.S. 1952, c. 270, s. 3). Civil Law lawyers were consulted in respect of civil law matters when they arose. Since the inception of the revision of the Statutes which began in 1965, the addition of experienced French-speaking civil law lawyers to the staff of the Legislation Section has made it possible to initiate working arrangements under which Bills prepared as described above are reviewed by such French-speaking civil law lawyers to ensure as far as possible
7576

that each of the two language versions of a Bill accurately expresses the substance of the other, and so that the implications of the proposed legislation in terms of its application to the common law and civil law may be fully appreciated and assessed. Plans are now being worked out that will formalize these arrangements and extend them to all Bills that are drafted in the Legislation Section. The ultimate objective is the implementation, as soon as possible, of a system of dual-language drafting involving the preparation of draft Bills in English and French as part of a single process.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Minister of Finance can he now give us a report on the inquiry into the increases in the prices of gasoline and heating oil, a report which he has been promising to give for some considerable time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: HEATING OIL AND GASOLINE-STATEMENT ON PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. My officials have looked into the recent increases that have occurred in the prices of gasoline, oil and heating fuel. I understand that the explanation given by the industry is that the increases were made necessary by rising costs, chiefly salaries, wages and supplies.
However, before a judgment can be made on issues such as this more information is required about a number of related factors. It is not sufficient to know only the extent to which costs have risen. Increased productivity, for example, might enable an industry to absorb cost increases and thereby avoid the need for higher prices. Other relevant considerations include the levels of profitability and capacity at which industry is operating, its ability to attract capital, and the degree of domestic and foreign competition.

Mr. Speaker, those of us on this side who have some liking for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) have felt very much like commiserating with him during the course of the past few weeks because of the embarrassment and difficulties in which he has found himself. I think many of us on this side feel that he is accident prone and Canada has a star-crossed minister.
Some of my colleagues tell me that from time to time the Minister of Finance has given to the house a brilliant analysis of the state of the economy. I certainly have no reason to question that judgment of my colleagues. However, it seems to me that while the minister may be capable of making brilliant analyses of the state of the economy, the problem is that the conclusions he reaches and the courses of action he maps out often do not follow the analyses arrived at and are quite erroneous.
At the present time, for example, we are told by the minister what is the combination of circumstances and what are the sets of problems that are causing difficulty in our economy. Then, as a follow-up, he presents us with fiscal measures, with a tax bill that in trying to deal with one set of problems in the economy will cause harm in other ways. It will cause harm by bringing about higher levels of unemployment than we have already, and they are already cause for concern. It

will bring about a further slow down in economic growth. When we look at the indices for last year we see that in terms of constant dollars there was last year very little economic growth in Canada.
I realize that because other hon. members have spoken in this debate, at the resolution stage and on the bill that was defeated, much of what I will say will be repetitious; but I do not apologize for that. I happen to have been connected with Jesuit institutions at one time, and one pedagogical rule that the Jesuits like to emphasize-perhaps I could express it in Latin-is repetitio matur studiurum est, which means that repetition is the mother of learning.
In the case of this government and the Minister of Finance I feel there is no need to apologize for repetition because it is one way of getting across to the government some of the fundamental, basic rules of economic performance. This government, surely, with all the high-priced help it has at its beck and call, should not have got itself in the position of levying increased taxation at a time when there are already strong indications of a slowdown in economic growth, an increase in unemployment, and so on. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will repeat quite a number of things without the slightest wish to apologize.
We are given to understand by the minister that the purpose of the bill now before us, the bill which the press has been referring to as tax bill mark III, is to combat the fires of inflation that are burning in Canada. I certainly agree that we have serious inflation at the present time. An increase in the cost of living of 4.5 per cent in two successive years is hardly a matter about which to be complacent.
The rate of inflation that exists in this country exceeds that of the United States, despite the fact that the economy of the United States is being overstrained and overreached much more than ours. Our neighbour to the south is fighting a war the cost of which approximates $25 billion or $26 billion a year. It is attempting to implement domestic policies and programs which are every bit as comprehensive as those of the government of Canada. It is maintaining a military presence not just in southeast Asia but on the continent of Europe on a scale proportionately higher than ours.
Despite all this, in the United States they have managed to keep the rate of inflation somewhat lower than that which prevails in Canada. I might add that on top of this they
March 13. 1968

have been increasing the money supply at a faster rate than was the case in Canada last year. Despite all these things, inflation is burning away very much more dangerously here than there, which makes one ask how this can be possible. I have already made my remonstrances to the Minister of Finance that he should not be proposing to the house a bill which will have the effect of taxing away excess demand. I have already insisted, together with others, that there is no excess demand on goods and services in Canada at the present time. It is not that kind of inflation. This has been reasserted to the minister by members on this side of the house time and time again, but apparently he has not heard. He does not want to hear. Whatever the reason, he proceeds as though there is excess demand and he recommends taxation accordingly. The inflation we have in this country today has really very little to do with demand. Therefore the adding of taxes merely adds to the problem and adds to the cost of goods and services. This will be followed in short order by an increase in prices and a demand for increased wages.
Obviously, members would agree that the inflation we have in this country now is a cost induced inflation and the imposition of a surtax does nothing to cure the disease. There is a second negative effect as well. We will derive from this new tax an effect which is opposite to that which is really needed. The new tax will lower demand, which is not excessive now, and it will increase the amount of unutilized economic resources. It follows therefore, there will be a further increase in unemployment, a further slowing down of economic growth. I know that some members opposite found it amusing yesterday when the hon. member for York-South (Mr. Lewis) made the logical assertion, that the effect of the tax measure before us will be to bring about simultaneously both inflationary pressures and deflationary pressures.
In a sense, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that this is not possible. However, I feel it certainly can be said that the effect of this bill will be paradoxical in that it will increase costs, and in that sense will be inflationary, while at the same time the effect will be to reduce employment and cause a greater under-utilization of our economic resources. In that sense it will be deflationary. The net effect certainly will be undesirable.
As I understand the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), he advances as an argument for this surtax the assertion that it will enable

the government to come close to balancing its budget, and therefore will remove the necessity for the government to go to the bond or money market to obtain funds. This will remove some of the pressures on the money-market. I do not wish to be critical in this respect, because there has been an excessive demand on the money market. This government is not the only cause of it. I do not believe there is any reason for criticism of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for saying, as he did, that the actual increase in expenditures at the federal level has been much less, in percentage, than the rate of increase of expenditures by provinces and municipalities. I agree with the Prime Minister.
There is nothing new in this phenomenon which is very apparent in the United States federal system and, I would suspect, in other federal systems throughout the world. The fact is that provincial governments have been increasing their expenditures rapidly. Perhaps this is the result of greater urbanization or industrialization, the great increase in the birth rate, and so on. All of these things necessitate greater expenditures on education and municipal services. The fact is that provincial governments have been spending more and more money and have been going to the money market more often for larger and larger amounts. This has nothing to do, it would seem, with political ideology, but I certainly do not wish to criticize the Prime Minister for having pointed out these facts to hon. members.
I agree it is too simple to criticize this government's spending which, I must concede, in so far as its rate of increase is concerned has been kept down to a greater extent than that of provincial or local governments. What should be looked at, in my opinion, is the rate of increase in spending in relation to that of the provinces, in relation to that of other industrialized states, in relation to the increase in gross national product and per capita income. All of these indices should be looked at before we attack the federal government for increasing its program of expenditures.
Of course taxes could be lowered. Of course public programs contemplated could be put aside. Of course public programs already implemented could be discontinued. All these things could be done; but if we took this option we should be prepared to admit that the consequences in social terms would be very disturbing. Within a short time private

But I do not wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no room for this government to cut costs. I do agree with the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales), who made a fine speech last evening outlining in detail some of the areas this government could explore with a view to cutting costs. Since he did such a good job in that regard, it is really unnecessary for me to do the same thing, as I had in mind to do. Very briefly, I should like to say that being on the public accounts committee with the hon. member it is becoming more and more obvious to us that if this government cared just a little more about administrative efficiency and cost cutting procedures a few million dollars might be saved for the public purse.
I am not sure of the position of my colleagues, Mr. Speaker, but I know my personal feeling is that there is nothing wrong with the announced intention of this government of putting a freeze on the recruitment of civil servants. It seems to me that in some departments a certain amount of extravagance has crept in as well as excessive recruitment. Some departments have adopted a sort of jet set attitude as to how to go about things. No doubt this is causing the administrative costs of some departments to rise higher than is really necessary. Probably at some future date, it will be necessary to increase the number of civil servants, but at the moment I agree that it is time for a period of consolidation and tightening up.
I think the hon. member for Wellington South pointed out, and if he did not I recall reading it in the Auditor General's report, that since 1962 there has been an increase in administrative personnel in the order of 40,000 and an increase in administrative costs in the order of $500 million. There are still many recommendations in the Glassco report that have not been implemented. The public accounts committee, working in conjunction with the Auditor General, has pointed out 450 instances in which administrative expenses could be pared. Of these 450 cases which have been resubmitted and resubmitted to the cabinet for action, only one third have been attended to. It is my personal opinion that that particular course of action at this time is a meritorious one.

It has also come to my attention that the Department of Public Works has become increasingly sloppy in its leasing of office space from private owners. The department has leased space which has then remained unused for months and months. Whole floors of office buildings in Ottawa are left idle, though all the while the rental is being paid. The department is engaging in leasing additional premises, even when other premises that have already been leased for some time remain underused. On top of all this, Mr. Speaker, a $40 million expenditure program in the Ottawa area is planned for this year to construct additional office space.
However, Mr. Speaker, I have digressed and I should like to return to the matter of price stability in our economy. In concluding my remarks in this connection the point I wish to make is simply this, that price stability, given the current set of conditions in our economy, cannot be achieved by fiscal or monetary measures. In fact such measures aggravate that set of conditions.
It seems to me that the steps that must be taken to achieve the goal of price stabilization must relate to the factors that are causing cost and price increases. Once we embark upon this goal we quickly find ourselves in the thicket or jungle of administered pricing, rising interest rates and, worst of all, something that has become chronic during the past 18 months or two years, the phenomenon known as the expectation of further inflation to come.
The inflation we are experiencing now, Mr. Speaker, is feeding on itself, and there is no question in my mind that this is the greatest single cause of the absolutely absurd interest rates existing in Canada today. Presumably those engaged in corporate enterprises and those who frequently deal on the money markets do not have very much faith in the capacity of this government to contain inflation, because they are proceeding to borrow, despite high rates of interest, thereby bringing about a continuing upward pressure on interest rates.
To give some indication how absolutely incomprehensible and absurd the interest rates in this country have become, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to three promissory notes I hold in my hand issued by one of the chartered banks to an individual who is personally known to me. The amount

From the reading I have been able to do it becomes increasingly apparent to me that the phenomenon known as investor confidence is often not connected with practical considerations; there are so many inconsistencies and paradoxes at work in connection with the international movement of capital that one does have cause to wonder, as George Brown did some years ago, what the "gnomes of Zurich" are doing. Listening to the Minister of Finance brought us no enlightenment.
As we know, the United States is itself in balance of payments difficulties. Foreign claims on United States gold far exceed United States gold balances and the situation is deteriorating further. One thing has come out of it. It has tied the Canadian dollar more closely than ever to the situation in the United States; it has tied the Canadian dollar more closely than ever to United States payments difficulties. Moreover it is my view that the set of problems which the United States faces in connection with its balance of payments situation is a chronic one which is likely to exist for a number of years, certainly as long as the war in Viet Nam lasts and as long as it maintains a powerful military presence in so many parts of the world.
The very fact that there has been a massive outflow of Canadian funds into United States equity stocks in the last four months is in itself some reason for the minister to feel despondent. I do not wish to begin now to make a case for exchange controls, but it is certainly a denial of common sense to be pleading on the one hand that the United States should not turn off the tap of investment and on the other hand to allow with apparent equanimity so large an outflow of Canadian investment funds into United States equity stock.
In conclusion, let me say we cannot support this tax bill because we are not convinced the minister has proved his case in relation to international monetary problems. In the second place, we cannot support the proposals for higher taxes because the present tax is based on a foundation which is inequitable, and to support any surtax calculated on such a base would be to compound inequity.

However, we have no intention of creating any unnecessary difficulties. The present situation of the government and of the country is of course troublesome because of the uncertainties internationally, and also because of something short of complete conviction about the government and its determination to carry out the appropriate policies.
We know that the United States dollar is under pressure because of balance of payments difficulties. We know too that part of the trouble here in Canada is doubts about the adequate determination or the ability of the

government of Canada to contain inflation. Some of us who have been watching the process have been rather interested in seeing the members of the government trying to set themselves up as the saviours of the country from a situation they largely created themselves.
However, I think there is an increasing area of agreement on some points between ourselves and hon. gentlemen opposite. Certainly the extent of the area of disagreement has been substantially reduced. It now seems to be agreed that the performance of Canada with regard to inflation has been bad. This now seems to be agreed on both sides of the house. This is what the Prime Minister said yesterday, as I understood him and he was not expressing any very different opinions from those that have been expressed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp).
I think it has been agreed, too, that as a result of this the competitive position of the country has been eroded, although there is some difference of opinion as to how serious the erosion has been. Our view on this side of the house is that it is urgent that inflation be controlled, that that is basic to the competitive position of Canadian industry, that to do this the Canadian government must have a budgetary policy that is related to the conditions of the economy, that it has not had this in recent times, and that the government has not yet demonstrated that it is prepared to adopt it.
I take the position that an appropriate budgetary policy, and the other recommendations laid down by the Economic Council of Canada, are not in themselves enough to achieve reasonable price stability and conditions of full employment, and I have been saying this for some time. When I say that the government has not yet shown any determination to adopt a budgetary policy appropriate to the conditions of the economy I simply refer to the decision made with regard to the medicare program, because certainly the reasons the Minister of Finance gave a year ago for deferring that program apply with far greater force today.
In October of last year the Minister of Finance gave some views about containing inflation. I believe these were the real, deeply held views of the minister with regard to the present situation and how it must be dealt with. On that occasion when he spoke to this house he stated most emphatically that if necessary he was quite prepared to create
March 13, 1968

some slack in the economy for a period of a year or two in order to remove the inflationary pressures.
It seems to me there is every indication, from what has happened since then, that in the view of the Minister of Finance and of the government substantial unemployment is necessary at the present time in order to meet the existing problem. To me, as I said then and as I have said since, this is an unacceptable solution.
It is true that in November, during the course of his mini-budget, the Minister of Finance made vague reference to some temporary program for encouraging restraint throughout the economy. It was an obscure reference, and when I questioned him in the house about it a few weeks ago, and asked what progress had been made with regard to the development of that program, he was not able to indicate that there had been any consultations outside the government. In fact I got the very distinct impression that very little indeed had been done with regard to exploring the possibilities of this, and certainly the statement made by the Prime Minister yesterday, in which he was unable to indicate the terms of reference or give any real description of the agency or the program that was to be followed, confirmed my view that in fact the government had been doing little or nothing on this program or this approach since last fall.
Certainly there had been no consultation. Certainly a good many months have been lost without the benefit of consultation. Now we are in the position where the best the government can say is that it is going to start consultations with the provinces and with other bodies to see what the terms of reference of this agency ought to be. This is as far as the government has taken us on this matter after all these months. Of course what all this does to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I would not know. I get the distinct impression that the government does not know either, because its members certainly avoided answering the question when it was asked earlier this afternoon.
I believe that a policy, a program to encourage restraint is essential. I recognize that there are substantial difficulties involved in any such program, but I say in all sincerity that to date the government has shown a complete failure to be able to maintain anything approaching price stability under conditions even approaching adequate employment.

I recognize, and am quite prepared to admit, that there was a good deal of slack in the economy when the government took over in 1963, although it started to move up after 1961. What I am saying now is that inflation has been out of proportion and excessive under this government ever since the rate of employment in this country reached anything approaching an acceptable figure. I do not say this simply to be abusive but rather to emphasize the point that surely, long since this, the government ought to have realized the need for other policies to at least supplement the policies it was following, and, that the policies it was following must lead either to continued uncontrolled inflation on the one hand, or to an eventual resort to deflation and unemployment on the other hand. Certainly at no time during its existence has this government demonstrated it is capable of maintaining an adequate rate of employment and price stability at the same time.
That is one reason that ever since I came here I have placed some emphasis on the need for a positive policy of restraint, guide lines, or whatever one might wish to call it. One can talk about the difficulty involved in a policy of guide lines. But what is the alternative? I think it has been demonstrated that this is difficult if there is inflation or excessive unemployment. This is not a problem just of this year; it is a problem of the times and a problem with which the government ought long since to have been wrestling. I cannot assess the Prime Minister's statement of yesterday. No one in the house nor in the country can assess it because it is so vague. No one knows what it means. All I can hope is that the government finally means business and is determined to move ahead in the area of encouraging a policy of restraint throughout the Canadian economy.
I think it is extraordinary that no serious move has been made in this direction long before this, because we now learn that the governor of the Bank of Canada has been urging the government for more than a year to adopt some such measure as this. In view of what had been happening, in view of the excessive increase in the cost of living and in view of the price level for not a matter of a year but for two or three years, I suggest there has been grave negligence on the part of the government in not heeding the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada in this respect.

If the minister wishes to quote my remarks that is one thing, but I wish he would not interpret them.
Certainly I believe it is agreed that these taxes add to the costs and the upward pressure on costs. They could only be considered

inflationary in that they tend to reduce effective demand. It seems to be pretty well agreed, however, that demand is not excessive now. We do not have an overheated economy. I do not hear anyone arguing that the Canadian economy is overheated. We do have idle resources, particularly human resources. Canada seems to be getting more of these as the months go by. We have a growing number of unemployed. We have falling profit margins and a further reduction in effective demand is likely to add to the difficulties of the country.
I assume that the Minister of Finance is concerned first of all about establishing financial responsibility by balancing his budget and reducing the demands on the capital markets. I assume also that he wishes to reduce inflationary pressures. When we discuss these matters we do so under some difficulty because we have not had a full budgetary presentation; we ought to have. Of course we are involved in a most extraordinary procedure in which these tax measures have been presented to the country and subsequently to the house. My point today is that we are not considering these proposals in the context of a full budgetary presentation, which would inform us at least what the minister's estimates were about growth, what his assumptions were when he computed his tax levels and things of that sort. So, to a considerable extent we are working in the dark. I hope the minister is not completely in the dark also. Certainly we do not have full information when we discuss these things now.
We do know that the current rate of the economic growth of the country is only about half the optimum or indeed the necessary rate of growth which the Economic Council of Canada has prescribed. We do know that if the country were growing at the optimum rate of growth, if this were conceivable under present circumstances, there would be substantial amounts of additional revenue and a great deal more than what the proposed 3 per cent surcharges would produce during the coming year, which is estimated to be $150 million. The difference between my position and that of the Minister of Finance in respect of his bill is about $150 million net. Of course a relatively slight increase in the rate of growth of the country would produce more than this. Apparently it is not possible for the Minister of Finance to contemplate measures to stimulate the economy, reduce the amount of unemployment and secure additional revenue in that way. The other day the Minister of Finance said, if I interpreted him correctly and he will correct me if I am wrong, that my suggestion that there was no need for the imposition of surcharges on taxes, because we could follow the alternative of deferring the repayment of the refundable tax and obtain additional savings, would put too big a restraint on the review board. No doubt the minister will try, and I am sure he will try as long as he is there. I want to say in all sincerity that it is not my purpose to make light of the difficulties that exist. I am really trying to discuss this matter in a serious way.
It is my hope that the government is not so discouraged about maintaining something like full employment along with a reasonable degree of price stability that from time to time it feels it has to create a substantial amount of unemployment in order to return to conditions of stability. As I understand it, the purpose of the agency that is being established is to try to reconcile or make it easier to achieve these two goals.
Yesterday the Prime Minister spoke about the increase in provincial expenditures and said that they were growing more rapidly than those of the federal government. There have been large increases in expenditures in the fields of education, health and welfare. This is true right across the country; it is not just true of one provincial government. This is the general situation I think in which provincial governments find themselves. Indeed the Economic Council of Canada has expressed the view that it is economically desirable that the Atlantic provinces should spend more than they have been able to spend, especially on such matters as education, highway improvement and other measures.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
However, I think it is quite correct to say that the provinces today have relatively little flexibility in their financial position. As a result of programs, some sponsored by the federal government, such as the hospital plan, and others, programs designed to equalize educational opportunities throughout the particular province, and so on, the provinces are involved in programs they have adopted

which have a very substantial annual built-in escalation. The present government has added to this problem by proposing quite recently that the provinces go ahead with another substantial program with a large annual built-in escalation.
The main point I wish to emphasize is that it does not help at all to point to the increase across the board in the expenditures of the provinces. The forecast made by the tax structure committee, sponsored by the federal government and the provinces, indicated that on the basis of programs then existing the provincial governments would move into positions of increasing deficit whereas the federal government would move into a position of increasing surplus. The lesson I draw from all this is the need for genuine consultation between the federal government and the provinces with regard to priorities. We have not yet had this. The process of consultation has really been considerably discredited by the federal government through insisting on going ahead with, for example, the medicare program, although eight of the ten provinces said they did not approve of the program and it was not the form of medicare program that they wanted.
Certainly a great and urgent need in Canada today is stability and growth. Surely that is where we must put the emphasis. It is not that economic growth is an end in itself. I think a country like ours has to have in mind higher purposes than this. We must think in terms of the quality of Canadian life. I do not believe in the process of cutting back just for the sake of cutting back. Certainly we want to get rid of waste. Certainly we must consider the position of the taxpayer.
I believe that the government has an active role to play in development, and equalizing opportunity and providing better services to the people. But surely we can agree that all of this has to come from economic growth. Economic growth will make it possible for us to do these things. We must therefore think in terms of an expansion of employment and increasing productivity. As I said, I cannot accept the principle that we need substantial unemployment to be rid of inflation. We are not in the position of having an overheated economy.
There are economic situations in which it is difficult to achieve full employment, but ordinarily this is not the case when the United States economy is growing in strength as it has been doing. Latterly we have not been doing as well as they have. In addition to all this, as I say, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me
March 13, 1968

that the government has been putting additional and unnecessary pressures on the provinces.
Therefore in summary I would say that in the existing circumstances we should not adopt policies which have the effect of creating additional unemployment, when there is already more unemployment than we want to see. We must recognize that an adequate rate of growth is essential to a satisfactory solution of our economic problems. We must bear in mind also the effect of these policies on areas of slow growth in the country.
Certainly the government must practise restraint. I suggest that it must consult with the provinces to work out priorities, and not simply dictate policies to the provinces. We should all be trying to work toward positions of greater flexibility so that this and other governments can respond more adequately to the changing conditions of the economy. We need to adopt a budgetary policy related to the needs of the economy, bearing in mind the priorities in the country. Therefore, I hope the government will get really busy with the program of encouraging restraints in our economy. I hope it will take really seriously the views of the Bank of Canada in this respect, and not merely the views that I have been expressing.
I think the failure of the policies of the government with regard to inflation has been long since apparent. I believe it was a grave mistake for the government not to heed the advice of the Bank of Canada far sooner than it did. The minister seemed to feel the need of some such policy last fall; but even now, more than a year after the governor of the Bank of Canada recommended the policy and many months after the Minister of Finance suggested that he was working toward such a policy, the government is unable to describe to the house the terms of reference of the agency. Even now there has been no consultation by the government with those outside the government with regard to how this program is going to work.
So we need a demonstration of restraint. The government has an opportunity to give the country a demonstration of restraint. We have a responsibility in connection with the unemployed and the maintenance of economic growth. Therefore, sir, in my opinion the surcharges are not necessary to meet the current emergency. I think rather that the government should put more emphasis on restraint and should defer the repayment of the refundable portion of tax rather than resort
Income Tax Act
to additional taxation, which will have the effect of imposing a further restraint on the growth of the economy and will tend to further increase unemployment.
So, Mr. Speaker, I urge the members of the house to oppose the measures put forward by the minister relating to surcharges, on the ground that they are not appropriate to the conditions that exist and they are burdens which are not required to be imposed on the Canadian people at the present time. Also in passing I cannot urge too strongly upon the government its responsibility to proceed seriously and conscientiously with the program of encouraging restraints throughout the economy.

He suffers from the restrictions imposed by his own view of economic affairs and also from the restrictions imposed by all of those persons who occupy comfortable pews in Canada at the present time.

The estimates for the Department of National Defence for the coming fiscal year total $1,700 millions. We could have saved at least $700 million of this for a starter had we withdrawn from the NATO and NORAD agreements. This is another reason for my opposition to the bill before us.
I am also opposed to the bill because the government of Canada has refused to use the Bank of Canada to provide the social capital required by federal, provincial and municipal governments for social investment, such as housing, hospitals, schools and other necessary facilities required by governments.
In conclusion, I wish to philosophize to a modest extent in order to place my ideas before the house. I fully appreciate the minister's difficulties occasioned by government policy, his own ideas on economics and the fact that society's technology shapes the lives and the understanding of citizens. The technology of our times, while it is air-conditioned and automated, is still essentially capitalist in its structure and logic. We have more comfort today, but after talking to the dozens of people I meet I question whether the people as a whole are any happier than their parents were 50 years ago; in many cases they have lost their purpose in life, lost their zest for undertaking things and lost their community identity because of the increasing size of our cities.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext: That is the truest thing you have ever said.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR SURCHARGE
speechtext:
Instead of the obvious
exploitation of years past, we have developed a comfortable capitalism which imposes new but more effective forms of social control. However, I cannot resist saying that despite our level of material prosperity, capitalism continues to institutionalize injustice and corrupt the potentialities of human beings. The capitalist system, with all its improvements, has succeeded in seducing the minds of many people who live in greater security and comfort, with the result that the status quo is granted a spurious consent. Individuals are inclined to identify themselves with the existence which is imposed upon them from above and are indoctrinated by the conditions under which they live and think, but are unable to transcend. In my opinion, the unrealized potentialities of many people remain undeveloped, due to an overabundance of goods and services which satisfy their
Division
immediate material needs, rendering them incapable of developing the aesthetic side of life which is the foundation of human happiness.
If government policies were designed to give effect to my proposals, that is, to stop the war in Viet Nam, to stop wasteful expenditure on defence and to use the Bank of Canada for social capital, I am confident we would be able to provide a material cultural environment which would enable all Canadians to understand the truth about life, to appreciate goodness wherever found and to enjoy beauty in all its forms.
